title: Left-tailed one-sample Z-test for supplier defect proportion
scenario_markdown: A hardware manufacturing plant has historically experienced a defect rate of $p_0 = 0.20$ ($20\%$) among mechanical switches sourced from a legacy vendor. A new supplier guarantees that its upgraded manufacturing process produces a defect rate strictly lower than $20\%$. Quality control inspects a random sample of $n = 200$ switches from the trial shipment and discovers $x = 28$ defective units (sample proportion $\hat{p} = 28/200 = 0.14$). Test at the $\alpha = 0.05$ significance level whether the defect rate is significantly lower than $0.20$ ($H_0: p = 0.20$ vs $H_1: p < 0.20$).
assumptions: np_0 = 200(0.20) = 40 >= 10 and n(1 - p_0) = 200(0.80) = 160 >= 10, justifying the standard normal Z approximation
Independent random sample of mechanical switches from the shipment lot
Standard error for testing is calculated under the null hypothesis using p_0 = 0.20

stages.prompt_markdown: Calculate the standard error under the null hypothesis $SE_0 = \sqrt{\frac{p_0(1 - p_0)}{n}}$ and the standardized test statistic $Z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{SE_0}$.

options.hint_markdown: In hypothesis testing for proportions, the standard error must be evaluated under the null hypothesis using $p_0 = 0.20$, not the sample proportion $\hat{p} = 0.14$.
The sample proportion $\hat{p} = 0.14$ is below the null value $0.20$, so the numerator $\hat{p} - p_0 = 0.14 - 0.20 = -0.06$ is negative.
Do not forget to take the square root of the variance term $\frac{0.20 \times 0.80}{200} = 0.0008$.

stages.explanation_markdown: Under the null hypothesis, $p = p_0 = 0.20$. The null standard error is $SE_0 = \sqrt{\frac{0.20 \times 0.80}{200}} = \sqrt{0.0008} \approx 0.028284$. The standardized test statistic is: $$Z = \frac{0.14 - 0.20}{0.028284} = \frac{-0.06}{0.028284} \approx -2.1213 \approx -2.12$$

options.hint_markdown: Because $H_1: p < 0.20$ is a one-tailed (left-tailed) test, do not double the tail area.
A left-tailed test measures the area to the left: $P(Z \le -2.12)$, which is the small tail $0.0170$, not $1 - 0.0170$.
The $p$-value is the probability area from the standard normal CDF, not the $Z$-score itself.

stages.explanation_markdown: For a left-tailed test, the $p$-value is the lower-tail probability $P(Z \le -2.1213)$. Using standard normal distribution tables or Excel `=NORM.S.DIST(-2.1213, TRUE)`, we obtain $p = 0.01695 \approx 0.0170$.

stages.prompt_markdown: At the $\alpha = 0.05$ significance level, state the test decision and managerial conclusion.

options.text_markdown: Reject $H_0$: Because $p = 0.0170 < 0.05$ (and $Z = -2.12 < -1.645$), there is sufficient statistical evidence that the new supplier's defect rate is significantly lower than $20\%$.
Fail to reject $H_0$: Because $p = 0.0170 < 0.05$, the sample result is considered normal random variation.
options.hint_markdown: When $p \le \alpha$, the result is statistically significant and we reject $H_0$.

options.text_markdown: Accept $H_0$: We have proven that the true defect rate is exactly $14\%$.
options.hint_markdown: A sample proportion $\hat{p} = 0.14$ is a sample estimate, not the population parameter; rejecting $H_0$ supports $H_1$, rather than accepting $H_0$.

options.text_markdown: Inconclusive: A sample size of $n = 200$ is too small to make a decision about a proportion.
options.hint_markdown: With $n p_0 = 40 \ge 10$ and $n(1 - p_0) = 160 \ge 10$, the normal approximation is fully satisfied and the sample size is ample.

stages.explanation_markdown: Comparing the $p$-value to the significance level: $p = 0.0170 < 0.05$. Equivalently, the test statistic $Z = -2.12$ falls in the rejection region ($Z \le -1.645$). We reject $H_0$ and conclude that there is statistically significant evidence that the new supplier's defect rate is below $0.20$.
